help.text:
Kaleidoscope local memory runtime

Usage:

AGENT -- the whole surface an agent needs. Two verbs, one door.

  kscope call search                         read;  one JSON request on stdin
  kscope call remember                       write; one JSON request on stdin
  kscope schema remember                     the write contract, before writing
  kscope schema [OPERATION]                  every operation this build has

  Those two resolve the vault from this directory. Name another one with
  `--profile`, which is what an editor or harness is started with:

  kscope call --profile <NAME> search
  kscope call --profile <NAME> remember

Everything below is an OPERATOR command: setup, inspection, and vault
lifecycle, run by a person or an installer and not by the agent using the
vault. `search` and `remember` are the only two published as MCP tools, and
the only two an agent is ever expected to choose between.

OPERATOR -- what this build is

  kscope --help
  kscope --version
  kscope model
  kscope gate
  kscope activate
  kscope licences
  kscope public-contract

OPERATOR -- bring a vault into existence

  kscope init [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope init <ROOT> <RFC3339_CREATED_AT> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope init-profile <NAME> <ROOT> <RFC3339_CREATED_AT> [process-local|durable-local]

OPERATOR -- profiles, a named non-secret pointer to one vault

  kscope profile create <NAME> <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope profile import <NAME> <ROOT> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope profile list
  kscope profile show <NAME>
  kscope profile remove <NAME>
  kscope profile launch <NAME>

OPERATOR -- which vault a command that names none resolves to

  kscope where
  kscope where --root-only

OPERATOR -- maintain a local vault

  kscope vault-migrate <ROOT>
  kscope vault-verify <ROOT> [--cross-backend]
  kscope vault-preview <ROOT>
  kscope vault-delete <ROOT>

OPERATOR -- encrypted repository vaults, a frozen macOS preview

  kscope vault-create <REPOSITORY> <RFC3339_CREATED_AT>
  kscope vault-open <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-close <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-recover <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-export-device <REPOSITORY> <NEW_PACKAGE_DIRECTORY>
  kscope vault-import-device <PACKAGE_DIRECTORY> <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-encrypted-preview <REPOSITORY>
  kscope vault-encrypted-delete <REPOSITORY>

OPERATOR -- run an engine for an agent, addressed three ways

  kscope mcp --profile <NAME>
  kscope serve --profile <NAME>
  kscope context --profile <NAME>
  kscope call --profile <NAME> <OPERATION>

  kscope mcp [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope serve [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope context [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope call <OPERATION> [process-local|durable-local]

  kscope mcp <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope serve <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope context <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> [process-local|durable-local]
  kscope call <ROOT> <WORKSPACE_ID> <PRINCIPAL_ID> <JOURNAL> <OPERATION> [process-local|durable-local]

The four commands that address a vault accept the four ids or none of them.
Naming none resolves them: KSCOPE_ROOT, else `.kaleidoscope/` under the
repository's main checkout, else `.kaleidoscope/` under the working directory --
and then the vault's own workspace record for the workspace, principal and
journal, so naming the root names all four. KSCOPE_WORKSPACE,
KSCOPE_PRINCIPAL and KSCOPE_JOURNAL override that record field by field, and
are how a vault holding more than one workspace is disambiguated.

Arguments always win, and win completely: an invocation naming the four ids
never reads the environment at all. That is what keeps every existing caller
byte-identical.

A resolved root that is not a vault is REFUSED by those four commands, naming
the path and where the path came from. They never create one: `kscope init` is
the only way a vault comes into existence, because a wrong root is not an
error, it is a different vault.

Init itself accepts the same two shapes. Naming ROOT and RFC3339_CREATED_AT is
unchanged in every respect, and is what a harness uses when a vault's created_at
has to be controlled. Naming neither resolves the root by the rules above, uses
the current time, and defaults to process-local -- durable-local fresh-root
initialization is refused before any effect, so it is asked for rather than
defaulted to. The resolved root and its provenance are printed on stderr,
unprompted.

A resolved root that is ALREADY a vault is refused too, and nothing there is
touched: a second init on an existing root mints a fresh workspace inside it,
and a vault holding two workspaces can no longer be addressed without naming
one. The refusal reports the ids it already has.

The resolved form also ensures the repository ignores the vault. `git
check-ignore` decides whether an existing rule already covers it, in which case
nothing is written; otherwise one commented rule is APPENDED, never reordering
or rewriting the file, and never adding a trailing newline the file did not
have. Outside a git repository nothing is written and no repository is created;
the vault is simply reported as not ignored. What was done is named on stderr
and in the gitignore field on stdout.

A version-1 profile is a non-secret pointer to one existing vault identity. It
stores an absolute root, workspace, principal, journal and durability under the
platform configuration directory's `kaleidoscope/profiles`, or exactly under
KSCOPE_PROFILE_HOME when that override is set. Profile names are portable and
path-safe; profile files are atomic, owner-only on Unix and validated against
the vault each time they are loaded. `profile import` derives the identity from
the selected vault; `profile create` verifies the explicit tuple. Neither one
creates or relocates canonical vault data.

`init-profile` is the native fresh-bootstrap primitive. It initializes the
explicit root, then writes the named profile. If the second step fails, it does
not delete the committed vault; the refusal reports the exact root and a
machine-readable recovery argv for `kscope profile import`. Durable-local is
never silently downgraded and remains refused before initialization effects.

`profile launch` prints a versioned stdio launch descriptor pointing directly
at this absolute engine executable with `mcp --profile NAME`. The descriptor
names only `search` and `remember` and contains no vault coordinates or secret.
Explicit four-coordinate invocations remain the compatibility authority and do
not read KSCOPE_PROFILE_HOME.

The where command prints the address these rules resolve to, as JSON, and
resolves nothing else. Every command that resolved rather than was told also
prints the same on stderr, unprompted, because a caller relying on a default
cannot check a root it did not type. stdout stays exactly what it was.

The licences command prints the attribution for third-party material this
executable redistributes inside itself. The embedded embedding table is
MinishLab's, under MIT, and MIT requires its notice to accompany every copy --
which a one-file release cannot do with a NOTICE beside the binary. `licenses`
is accepted as a spelling. The output states what it does not yet cover.

The model command prints one JSON object naming the semantic embedding model
this executable carries, its table dtype, and the SHA-256 of its two files, or
reports that this build has none. A release must report one: the release
installer refuses a package whose executable does not.

The gate command prints one JSON object naming what this build carries of the
alpha entitlement gate: enforcing or absent, the commands the gate refuses,
and where a key file would be read from. It reads no key, opens no vault and
reports no authorization decision. The gate never refuses this command, so an
operator holding a refused binary can still find out why it was refused.

The activate command is how a machine becomes entitled. It takes the key from
KALEIDOSCOPE_API_KEY, from the key file, or from standard input; stores it at
the path the gate command reports, so an engine a host starts with an empty
environment finds it; and waits for the verdict rather than leaving the next
command to discover an empty cache. It is never gated, because a gate across
the only route to becoming entitled is closed to everyone not already through
it. It exits 0 only when the key reached the disk: a key that could not be
stored is a refusal naming the path, and a build carrying no gate refuses as
well rather than reporting an activation it did not perform.

`-h` and `-V` are accepted as short forms of `--help` and `--version`.

The public-contract command prints a small source-free JSON seed for release
contract generation. It opens no vault and loads no model.

The vault-recover command reads a JSON object containing recovery_key from
stdin. The two delete commands require their preview command's
confirmation_token in a JSON object on stdin. Encrypted repository vaults are
a frozen macOS-preview feature.

The optional serve command uses a Unix-domain socket and is unavailable on
non-Unix platforms. The stdio mcp command and process-scoped call command do
not depend on it.

The vault-migrate command builds the storage engine's index over a vault
written by the older fs-v0 engine. It creates, moves, copies and deletes no
content file, re-runs safely, works on a vault whose journal has rotated, and
is undone by deleting one file -- until the first write through the engine.
Run vault-verify after it and before writing. Neither command reads the
journal, so both work on a vault this executable cannot otherwise open.

The context command reads one search JSON request from stdin and prints only
the concise model-visible memory text. call search returns the bounded public
result, including final rank and fused score on selected hits; private
policy/ranker feature vectors, the signed decision payload and engine
diagnostics are omitted. The documented public workflow has no supported
outcome-attribution path until a future authenticated manager/controller
interface exchanges a keyed opaque handle. This is an API contract, not an
authentication claim about the local vault.

The call command reads one JSON request from stdin. OPERATION is one of:

  AGENT     search | remember
  OPERATOR  feedback | memory_lifecycle | memory_import | address_maintenance
            maintenance | ontology | doctor

Only the two agent verbs are published as MCP tools. search merges what were
recall, compile and read_memory: a query ranks and a memory_id addresses. A
ranked search always writes the exposure row and bounds the served set --
ledger: false was a second door and is refused, so a measurement that must not
write to a vault has to clone it first. Its four knobs are top_k,
candidate_pool, bfs_depth and max_facts, each with a published default and
ceiling.

The schema command prints one OPERATION's full descriptive parameters and
closed values. MCP derives a versioned compact, omission-first inputSchema from
the same operation semantics. The two preserve the same non-null machine
constraints but are intentionally not byte-identical: the native decoder
accepts legacy explicit null while MCP omits absent optionals. Pass no OPERATION
to list them.

Exit codes. 0 means applied: everything asked for happened, and for a remember
carrying items every submitted item was written. 2 means refused: nothing was
applied, stdout carries a refusal envelope rather than a per-item report, and
the repair is to fix the request and re-send it whole. 3 means applied in part:
the response says status partial, some items were written and at least one was
not, and stdout carries results -- one entry per submitted item, in submission
order, each with its own status and reason. Re-send only the items whose status
is not a write; re-sending the batch re-submits memories the vault already
holds. 3 exists so that a caller reading $? can tell those two repairs apart
without parsing the body, which is the parse an exit code exists to avoid.

operation_schemas.name: remember
operation_schemas.text:
remember

Write memory: create, update, or delete one, or create several in order. Write when you learn something, not only when you are told to: if you had to read code, run an experiment, or rule out a wrong answer to establish it, that is exactly what the next session would pay to rediscover.

AGENT VERB — published as an MCP tool.

  mode (required)
    What this write does.
    closed — one of:
      create  write a new memory
      update  replace an existing memory's content and facts
      delete  logically delete one memory
  memory_id (optional)
    Required for update/delete; for create it is derived from the retry identity.
  content_md (optional)
    Markdown beginning with `# ` for create/update; omitted for delete and for a batch, which carries its markdown per item.
  semantic_delta (optional)
    The validated semantic structure committed with create/update, with at least one fact; omit for delete.
      context (optional) — The verbatim source text this memory was extracted from. Stored so a reader can check the extraction against what was said; it is never parsed.
      contradicts (optional)
      corrections (optional) — Corrections to what the vault already holds. Nothing gates a correction — a system where fixing a memory is harder than writing one accumulates errors.
        handle (required) — The handle the correction is about.
        says (required) — What is being corrected.
      entities (optional) — Every entity your facts name. Declare all of them or none: a half-declared memory resolves half its mentions on a worse probe. A DATE IS NEVER AN ENTITY — times go in `occurred_at`, a fact's `from`/`until`, or an `about` key.
        is (required) — A one-line gloss. REQUIRED, and it is not documentation — it is what the matcher probes with. `opus 5` alone matches on four characters; `opus 5 | model | Anthropic language model` is what actually finds the node you meant.
        kind (required) — Known here: artifact, capability, concept, doc, event, metric, model, org, person, place, practice, tool. New values are accepted. A novel kind only shifts kind_compat's score, and it is useful immediately when it arrives with its is_a edge. Minting one is 3-zone threshold.
        n (required) — The surface your facts refer to this entity by, spelled as they spell it.
      evidence (optional) — Inspectable local evidence references; never hidden model reasoning.
        digest (optional) — Optional content digest of the referenced evidence.
        kind (required) — Evidence class, such as `file`, `test`, or `user_statement`.
        reference (required) — Locator, such as a path, URL, or identifier.
      facts (required)
        about (optional) — Qualifiers on this fact. Each key's declared class decides how its value is read: a referential value is resolved against the graph exactly as a mention is, an ordinal value is checked against the closed scale, a literal value is validated and not resolved.
          <any key> — A string for a referential or ordinal key, a number for a quantity, or a `{t, grain}` object for a time.
          <key> — Known here: amount, certainty, degree, for, instrument, priority, scope, source, unit, when. New values are accepted. A novel key only shifts matching — but without a declared class KScope cannot tell whether to resolve its value or validate it. Minting one is 3-zone threshold, and a declared class — referential, ordinal or literal.
        basis (optional) — background = the model knows it; the text does not say it; implied = the text presupposes or entails it; stated = the text says it. Closed: it feeds the base term of the confidence formula, base(basis) × corroboration ÷ contention × decay (design §4.2). [one of: background, implied, stated]
        evidence (optional)
        from (optional) — When this fact starts being true. Absent inherits the memory's `occurred_at`.
          grain (required) — Which period `t` names. Send the grain the memory actually supported: `March` is `{"t": "2026-03", "grain": "month"}` and never `2026-03-01`. [one of: year, month, day, hour, instant]
          t (required) — The value at the grain below: `2026`, `2026-03`, `2026-03-15`, `2026-03-15T09`, or an RFC 3339 timestamp. The grain is read FIRST and selects the form this is decoded at; nothing infers the form from the value.
        mode (optional) — fact = a statement about the world; preference = what the subject would choose, other things equal; decision = a choice that was made and stands until something supersedes it; procedure = a reusable way of doing something; outcome = what happened when something was tried, attributable to it; event = something that occurred at a time. Closed: it feeds the decay rate, the default retrievability, and supersession eligibility. [one of: fact, preference, decision, procedure, outcome, event]
        object (required)
        predicate (required) — Known here: authored, avoids, blocked_by, caused, costs, decided, depends_on, instance_of, made_by, measured_at, owned_by, part_of, powers, prefers, stopped_using, strong_at, switched_to, uses, weak_at, worked_on. Refused, emitted by the fold: contradicts, justified_by, not_same_as, possibly_same_as, same_as, supersedes. New values are accepted. A novel verb only shifts the definition probe's score — but two predicates for one relation split every fact of it, so reuse before you propose. Minting one is 3-zone threshold, and a semantics proposal — means, from, to, many, over_time.
        subject (required)
        until (optional) — When it stops. Absent stays absent — it never inherits, because the memory default is a start and inheriting it as an end would close every open interval in the vault. — the same fields as `semantic_delta.facts[].from`
      memory_type (required) — Workspace ontology type. Reuse an accepted name rather than coining a near-synonym: types are append-only, so `user_preference` and `preference` would both persist forever.
      occurred_at (optional) — When this memory's facts are about. YOU resolve the time — `last Tuesday` becomes an absolute value with a grain, or this stays null. Kaleidoscope parses no date out of prose. A fact with no `from` of its own inherits this, and the claim records that it inherited. — the same fields as `semantic_delta.facts[].from`
      propose (optional) — Relations you believe you are inventing. Sending none is itself a claim — that the verbs you used already exist. A proposal is active immediately; it is what lets a relation supersede rather than accumulate.
        from (optional) — The declared domain kinds.
        inverse (optional) — Optional, and yours alone to supply: nothing computes an inverse from a definition, and a wrong one makes every claim readable backwards under a verb the vault never agreed to.
        many (required) — Whether one subject may hold several objects at once. It puts the object on the slot key, so it decides what may collide.
        means (required) — The definition. It dominates the matching probe — a proposal without one is a name, and names are low signal.
        over_time (required) — Whether supersession applies to this relation at all. [one of: event, state, immutable]
        rel (required) — Known here: authored, avoids, blocked_by, caused, costs, decided, depends_on, instance_of, made_by, measured_at, owned_by, part_of, powers, prefers, stopped_using, strong_at, switched_to, uses, weak_at, worked_on. Refused, emitted by the fold: contradicts, justified_by, not_same_as, possibly_same_as, same_as, supersedes. New values are accepted. A novel verb only shifts the definition probe's score — but two predicates for one relation split every fact of it, so reuse before you propose. Minting one is 3-zone threshold, and a semantics proposal — means, from, to, many, over_time.
        to (optional) — The declared range kinds.
      scope (optional) — Where this memory applies. An omitted axis matches every request; a set axis matches only that exact value.
        artifact (optional)
        branch (optional)
        project (optional)
      temporal (optional) — Validity interval. A memory whose `valid_until` has passed is not served.
        valid_from (optional)
        valid_until (optional)
      title (required) — The memory's title, in your words. It is not scraped out of `content_md` (ADR 0053): you already know the title you wrote, and recovering it by parsing the rendered form makes the display format load-bearing and mis-titles any memory whose body does not open with an H1.
  expected_version_id (optional)
    The active version update/delete is allowed to replace. Required for update/delete and omitted for create.
  items (optional)
    Several creates in one call, applied in order, instead of content_md/semantic_delta. Every item declares its own title and facts -- nothing is shared or inherited between them. Use it when you have already extracted several memories in one reasoning step; a batch does not invent IDs or a hidden supersession edge between items. An item this call cannot accept is refused on its own and the others are still written: the response reports it at its index with status `refused` and the reason, so repair that item and resend only it. That isolation is per-item VALIDATION. A field this schema does not name fails deserialization instead, which happens before any item is written and costs the whole call, so resend all of it.
      content_md (required)
      semantic_delta (required) — the same fields as `semantic_delta`

EXAMPLE — the smallest call this build accepts:
Every field this omits at the TOP level is optional. Nested ones are not: a field marked
(required) above is required as soon as you send the object it sits in. The one worth
adding first is `semantic_delta.entities` — declare EVERY surface your facts name, or
none of them, each with `n`, `kind` and `is`; without it the resolver matches on the bare
surface.

{
  "content_md": "# The payments client retries with exponential backoff\n\nA fixed delay re-sent every retry into the same overloaded window.",
  "mode": "create",
  "semantic_delta": {
    "facts": [
      {
        "object": "exponential backoff",
        "predicate": "uses",
        "subject": "payments client"
      }
    ],
    "memory_type": "decision",
    "title": "The payments client retries with exponential backoff"
  }
}

operation_schemas.name: search
operation_schemas.text:
search

Read memory in exactly one mode. A `query` ranks, bounds the served context, and writes an exposure row. A `memory_id` returns one exact current record, runs no ranking or filtering, and accepts none of the ranked controls.

AGENT VERB — published as an MCP tool.

  query (optional)
    Ranked selection: what to search for. Supply exactly one of query and memory_id.
  memory_id (optional)
    Addressed selection: the `mem_...` identity to return. It ranks, filters, and compiles no served set, so ranked-only controls below do not apply and supplying one alongside it is refused rather than ignored.
  top_k (optional)
    Ranked query only. Maximum memories to serve, in ranked order. It changes the amount of context the caller receives, so evaluations compare runs only at the same value. Omission uses the published default; values above the published ceiling are refused.
  candidate_pool (optional)
    Ranked query only. How many candidates each enabled retrieval channel may propose before the final served-set cut. It is independent of top_k. Omission uses the published default; values above the published ceiling are refused.
  ledger (optional)
    Ranked query only. Write an exposure-ledger row and bound the served set to maximum_context_bytes. It defaults to true and FALSE IS REFUSED, not silently upgraded: a caller that asked for a read-only search and quietly got a write would put a row into a store it believed it was only reading. So a ranked search is always a write, and a measurement that must not write has to clone the vault. Omit this field for memory_id, which writes no exposure row.
    closed — one of:
      true  write the required exposure row and apply the context bound
  maximum_context_bytes (optional)
    Ranked query only. The byte budget the served set is bounded to. Omission uses the published default.
  as_of (optional)
    Ranked query only. RFC3339 instant validity is evaluated at. Omitted means now, not `ignore validity`.
  scope (optional)
    Ranked query only. Restrict the served set to one project/branch/artifact. An omitted axis matches every memory.
      artifact (optional)
      branch (optional)
      project (optional)
  channels (optional)
    Ranked query only. Restrict which retrieval channels may contribute candidates. Omit for normal serving, which runs every channel; naming a subset is how a channel's contribution is measured.

schema_index.text:
kscope schema <OPERATION>

Two agent verbs, published as MCP tools:
  search
  remember

Operator commands, in no agent tool list:
  feedback
  memory_lifecycle
  memory_import
  address_maintenance
  maintenance
  ontology
  doctor

tools.description: Write to this user's persistent Kaleidoscope memory, the local vault `search` reads. Call it WITHOUT being asked whenever the user states a preference, accepts or rejects a decision, sets a standing constraint, corrects something you did or said, or a verified milestone produces an attributable outcome — anything a later session would otherwise have to rediscover. Do not wait for the words "remember this" and do not batch it all to the end of the task. It takes a STRUCTURED semantic delta, not free prose: `mode` is create, update or delete; a create or update carries `content_md` (markdown opening with `# `) and a `semantic_delta` whose `memory_type`, `title` and 1-32 `facts` of subject/predicate/object are all required, every entity is `{n, kind, is}` with `is` a mandatory matcher gloss, and update and delete additionally need `expected_version_id`. Dates are NOT entities — they belong in `occurred_at`, a fact's `from`/`until`, or `about.when`, resolved to an absolute value and a grain by you, because the store parses no date. Revise an earlier memory through `corrections` and `contradicts` rather than by appending a second memory; introduce a new relationship name through `propose`, which is active on arrival with no review queue. Send up to 20 memories extracted in one reasoning step as `items`, each self-contained. Do NOT store secrets, credentials, transcripts, ordinary file contents, or tentative brainstorming.

input_schema.description: H1; 1-32 facts; update/delete need expected_version_id; Batch: create-only/exclusive; rel/kind are open; active immediately; n/kind/is matcher gloss; entities/evidence32 propose8 corrections/contradicts16 f/because>=0 confidence/admission 0..1.

tools.name: remember

tools.description: Read this user's persistent Kaleidoscope memory: their prior decisions, stated preferences, standing constraints, corrections, reusable procedures and recorded outcomes, held in a local vault. Use it BEFORE starting a nontrivial task rather than after one, to recover context you would otherwise rediscover or ask the user for a second time, and to check whether a question has already been settled. Exactly one of two modes per call: a `query` is a natural-language ranked read that selects and bounds the served context and WRITES an exposure row, so it is a write and must not be freely replayed or cached; a `memory_id` returns that one exact current record, ranks and filters nothing, and refuses the ranked-only controls. `top_k` is protocol-defining rather than a page size — it decides the served shape, and ~5 is the intended size — while `candidate_pool`, `bfs_depth` and `max_facts` bound the work behind it. Do NOT use this as a file, code or web search: it searches remembered statements about this user's work, not file contents, and it reaches nothing outside the local vault.
tools.name: search
